tagline.text: A green island afloat at the center of the world's marine biodiversity

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱4,000–9,000 per person (per day, diving included)

children.text: A small volcanic island in the middle of the Verde Island Passage, between Luzon and Mindoro. This passage is called the "center of the center" of the world's coastal fish diversity, and the drop-off just off the island is one of the Philippines' premier wall-diving sites, where schools of fish and coral seem to explode into view in a strong current.
Verde Island is a volcanic island about
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes

south across the water from Batangas City, and administratively part of it. About 5,000 people live in the island's six villages — Liponpon, San Agapito, San Agustin East and West, San Andres, and San Antonio — and the highest point, Liponpon Peak, rises to about
above sea level. True to its name, the whole island is covered in green forest, and its coastline alternates between cliffs and small stretches of white sand.
What makes Verde Island special is the Verde Island Passage that surrounds it. American marine biologists Kent Carpenter and Victor Springer, in a study published in

, named this passage the "center of the center of the center" of coastal marine fish diversity. In other words, within the Coral Triangle, the world's richest region for reef life, this is the spot with the most fish species per unit area. The passage is home to more than 300 species of coral and protected species such as sea turtles, Napoleon wrasse, and giant clams.

As a narrow strait linking the South China Sea and the Sibuyan Sea, it has a strong current, and that current carries nutrients that feed schools of fish and soft coral. Because of this, the drop-off off the island is a place to see barracuda and jack schools, turtles, and vividly colored fan coral all at once — but it's also a spot best suited to divers experienced with current. In
, the five provinces bordering the passage — including Batangas and Mindoro — joined together to form the Verde Island Passage Marine Protected Area Network, and in
, the international ocean conservation group Mission Blue designated it a "Hope Spot."

Most travelers arrive by boat for a day of diving from a dive resort in Puerto Galera on Mindoro or Anilao in Batangas. Non-divers can spend a quiet day at Mahabang Buhangin, a roughly 1km white sand beach on the island's south side, a rock-cave passage running to the other side of the island, or a village homestay. It's recommended for intermediate-and-above divers, marine life photographers, and travelers looking for an uncrowded island.
The signature site: a coral wall dropping to over
deep around rocks that break the surface. The highlight is drift diving along the wall with the current, watching schools of fish and soft coral go by.

On days with strong current, barracuda and jacks circle in schools, and with luck you may meet a Napoleon wrasse or a sea turtle. Toward the lower part of the drop-off, large fan corals and sponges are spectacular.
The coral crevices are full of nudibranchs, sea slugs, shrimp, crabs, and small scorpionfish. The shallow coral gardens, with weaker current, are popular with macro photographers.
In the shallow coral areas at the island's edge, calm water lets even snorkelers see butterflyfish, damselfish, and coral reefs. Always go with a boat crew or guide.
A white sand beach about
1km
long, its name meaning "long sand." A good spot to rest between dives, or for non-divers to walk the beach and swim.
On one side of the island, a passage runs through a cave between the rocks to come out on the other side. Go with a local guide, timed to good tide conditions.
Spending a night in this lightly touristed fishing village lets you see the lights of boats crossing the passage, the stars, and fishing boats coming in early in the morning.

2–3 hours

The public boat for residents leaves once a day not from Batangas Port but from Tabangao Port (Tabangao Aplaya) in Batangas City, and takes about
1 hour 30 minutes
to reach the island. It usually departs around
9 AM
once full, and the boat back from the island leaves at
4 AM
the next day, so a same-day round trip isn't possible on the public boat. The fare is about
one way.

30–45 minutes
to Verde Island, while the ferry from Batangas port to Puerto Galera itself takes about

Dive resorts in Anilao also run Verde Island expedition dives. The boat ride is about
1 hour

From the end of the SLEX–STAR Tollway to Batangas port takes about

per day.

During the
June–October

rainy season, the southwest monsoon and typhoons roughen the passage, and the coast guard often suspends small-boat service. Dive shops frequently switch to sites closer to shore or cancel the expedition altogether. Current is driven more by the tide than the season, running especially strong around the spring tides near the full and new moon.

Lodging on Verde Island itself is limited to a handful of small resorts and village homestays, with modest facilities (about

per night). For that reason, most divers stay at Sabang Beach or Small La Laguna in Puerto Galera, or at a dive resort in Anilao, and visit Verde Island as a day trip. Choosing a diving package (lodging, meals, and diving included) gets you a comfortable stay for about
per person, per day.

On the island, meals are a simple seafood spread — the day's catch grilled or cooked as sinigang — and shops are small, so it's best to bring water and snacks from Batangas City. Batangas City is the home of Batangas lomi, thick noodles in a rich broth, so it's worth a bowl on the way to or from the port, and bulalo (beef bone-marrow soup) and strong kapeng barako coffee are also local specialties. If you stay in Puerto Galera, the restaurant strip at Sabang Beach offers a wide range of seafood dishes and Western food.

Because of the strong current, most shops require an Advanced certification or above and a certain amount of logged experience to dive the Verde Island drop-off. Beginners should ask for a site with weaker current first.
An SMB (surface marker buoy) and a whistle are essential for drift diving in current. If you don't have one, rent it from the shop.
For non-divers, the easiest and safest way to see the area is to join the dive boat as a snorkeler. Check the fare and which sites allow snorkeling in advance.
There are no ATMs on the island. Bring cash for your homestay, boat, and meals.
Electricity and phone signal on the island can be weak. Bring a power bank and a dry bag.
In the marine protected area, use reef-safe sunscreen, and don't wear gloves or collect any marine life.
Leave a comfortable margin before your flight out of Manila, since you shouldn't fly within
18–24 hours
of diving.
In island villages, electricity often relies on generators and solar power and is available only around
. If you need air conditioning, choose a resort with its own generator.

The Verde Island Passage is one of the strongest-current bodies of water in the Philippines. Downcurrents, upcurrents, and whirlpools can occur, so always follow your local guide, and don't push into the drop-off if you lack experience.
The passage is a shipping lane used by large cargo ships and ferries. Deploy your SMB as soon as you surface and wait for your boat.
The coast guard halts boat service in bad weather or when there's a typhoon warning. Build in a spare day when planning a trip to the island.
Always snorkel with a boat crew or guide, and stay close to the beach on days with current.
Environmental incidents can occur in the passage, as with the
oil spill from a tanker off Mindoro. Avoid entering the water if there's a marine pollution advisory, and check the latest notices.
Don't touch or step on coral and marine life, and carry out all your trash. The island is home to a living community, so ask before taking photos.
